schools.summary: Calvin thinks the chapter begins in the wrong place, the division interrupting one of the most touching scenes in the sacred volume just in the middle and separating Judah's irresistible appeal from its happy effect, whereas in the Hebrew Bible the section commences with that address and the whole runs as one narrative. Joseph had done violence to his feelings so long as he presented an austere countenance; at length the affection he had suppressed while breathing threatenings poured itself forth with the more abundant force, whence it appears that nothing cruel had before been harboured in his mind, and that it bursts forth in tears deserves more praise than an equable temper would. The stoics therefore speak foolishly in calling it an heroic virtue not to be touched with compassion — had Joseph stood inflexible, who would not have pronounced him iron-hearted? He commanded all men to depart not because he was ashamed of his kindred, since he afterwards permits the report to be carried to the palace, but because he would not make known their crime before many witnesses; and it was not the smallest part of his clemency to desire their disgrace wholly buried in oblivion.

Henry, whom Wesley follows almost word for word, reads the scene as a picture of grace. Judah and his brethren, waiting for an answer, could not but be amazed to discover, instead of the gravity of a judge, the natural affection of a brother. The private conversations of friends are the most free: when Joseph would put on love he puts off state, and it was not fit his servants should be witnesses of it — thus Christ manifests his loving-kindness to his people out of the sight and hearing of the world. The tears were the introduction to his discourse: he had dammed up this stream a great while, but now it swelled so high that he wept aloud, so that those whom he had forbidden to see him could not but hear him. Then abruptly, as one uneasy till it was out, he tells them who he is; they knew him only by his Egyptian name, and lest they suspect another of the same name he explains himself — I am Joseph your brother — which would both humble them for their sin and encourage them to hope for kind treatment.

Clarke fastens on the verb, which is very emphatic: it signifies to force one's self, to do something against nature. Joseph could no longer constrain himself to act a feigned part — all the brother and the son rose up in him at once and overpowered his resolutions; he felt for his father, realising his agony, and for his brethren, now at his feet submissive in distress. Clarke quotes Dodd, that the beauties of this chapter are so striking it would be an indignity to point them out, nothing in sacred or profane history being more highly wrought up.

Ellicott names what overpowered him: the picture Judah had drawn of his father's love for Benjamin, the thought that by separating them he might have made his father die of grief, and the sight of Judah offering to endure slavery for him. He cleared the room so that there might be no restraint on either side when he told them he was the brother they had condemned to slavery.

outliers.note: objects that the chapter division falls in the wrong place, cutting Judah's appeal off from its effect

2.pericope_label: I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?

schools.summary: Calvin turns the brothers' silence into a rule for dealing with the penitent. Although Joseph had given the clearest token of his mildness, yet when he told them his name they were terrified as if he had thundered against them; for while they revolve what they have deserved, his power seems so formidable that they anticipate nothing but death. Seeing them overcome with fear, he utters no reproach, but labours to calm their perturbation until he has rendered them composed and cheerful. So long as the offender is deaf to reproofs, or flatters himself, or excuses himself by hypocrisy, greater severity is to be used; but rigour should have its bounds, and as soon as he trembles under the sense of his sin, that moderation should follow which may raise him by the hope of pardon. The invitation to come near is, in Calvin's judgment, more efficacious than words: Joseph attempers his speech so that he mildly accuses and again consoles, but the consolation predominates, because he sees them on the point of desperation. Gill observes that the restraint Joseph had put on himself made the flood the greater and his voice the louder, and supposes they had kept their distance while he sat in state, so that the summons brought them near enough to discern in his face the features they had known.

Clarke is puzzled that the weeping carried as far as the palace, and answers it out of travel: Sir John Chardin says this is exactly the genius of the people of Asia, whose sentiments of joy or grief are properly transports, ungoverned and excessive, so that when anyone returns from a long journey or dies, his family burst into cries that may be heard twenty doors off. He allows two soberer readings — that the house of Pharaoh may mean the king's servants, such as those just dismissed, still within hearing, or that the report was afterwards brought to the palace. He also sets the scene beside Homer, where Ulysses discovers himself to Telemachus and tears till then restrained trickle down the cheeks of both.

Ellicott takes the last of Clarke's readings flatly: what the Egyptians and the house of Pharaoh heard was not the weeping but the news that his brethren had come. He finds much force in the assurance that Joseph was still their brother, for they stood speechless at finding the hated dreamer, on whose anguish they had looked unmoved, now ruler of a mighty empire. Keil reads the hearing the other way, that as soon as the rest were gone Joseph broke out into such loud weeping that the Egyptians outside could hear it; and he notices that Joseph asks after his father although twice told he was living, his filial heart impelling him to make sure once more, while the brothers were so smitten in conscience they could not utter a word.

5.pericope_label: It was not you that sent me hither, but God

schools.summary: Calvin calls this a remarkable passage, teaching that the course of events is never so disturbed by the wickedness of men but that God can direct it to a good end, and teaching also how we must consider providence. When men of inquisitive minds dispute about it they invent every absurdity in their power to sully the justice of God, and that rashness makes some pious men wish the doctrine concealed; yet a just measure must be kept, lest we encourage ignorance of what the word of God makes plain. Good men, afraid of exposing God's justice to the calumnies of the impious, resort to the distinction that God permits some things but does others — as if any liberty of action were left to men were he to cease governing. Away with that vain figment, Calvin says, that by permission only and not by will those evils are committed which God afterwards turns to good account: the vice dwells in the men, and the blame is theirs, but God works wonderfully through their means, that from their impurity he may bring forth his righteousness. Joseph was sold by his brethren for no reason but that they wished to ruin him, and the same work is ascribed to God for a very different end — God willing that Joseph should be as one dead for a short time, that he might suddenly bring him forth from the grave as the preserver of life. Gill guards the denial that they sent him: not absolutely, since they did sell him to the Ishmaelites, but comparatively, providence having overruled those events.

Clarke conjectures that father was a name of office in Egypt, signifying what prime minister does among us, Calmet remarking that among the Phoenicians, Persians, Arabians and Romans the title was given to officers of state; and he adds from Diodorus that the counsellors of the kings of Egypt were chosen out of the priesthood. He reads the words themselves with every emphasis: not you but God, not you that sold me but God who sent me; Egypt and Canaan must both have perished had not a merciful provision been made. Wesley draws the lesson that God's Israel is the particular care of God's providence, Joseph reckoning his advancement designed not so much to save a whole kingdom of Egyptians as to preserve a small family of Israelites; for the Lord's portion is his people, and whatever goes with others they shall be secured.

Ellicott agrees that this was a common title of the vizier of Oriental kings, and notices a smaller thing: the article is rarely found with Elohim in the history of Joseph, but wherever it is added it marks deep feeling in the speaker — it was the God whom their race had worshipped that had now interposed to save them. On the promise he weighs both nouns: to preserve a posterity is, in Hebrew, to put for them a remnant in the land, for during the famine many races probably dwindled away and the Hebrews, as sojourners in Canaan, would have been in danger of extinction; and where the first clause seems to forebode that few would survive, the word rendered deliverance, which signifies rather that which escapes, assures them of surviving in numbers enough to grow into a great nation. Keil renders the office Pharaoh's most confidential counsellor, and both he and Clarke note that earing is the old English for ploughing — though Clarke adds that the promise of no seed-time must be qualified, since the Egyptians afterwards came to buy seed.

outliers.note: refuses the distinction between what God permits and what God wills, holding that the blame rests wholly on the men while the deed is still God's

9.pericope_label: Haste, and bring my father down to Goshen

schools.summary: Calvin explains why Joseph presses his own greatness: in giving this command he speaks of his power in order to inspire his father with stronger confidence, since we know how dilatory old men are, and besides it was difficult to tear holy Jacob away from the inheritance divinely promised him. It may be asked why the old oracle did not occur to their minds, that they should be strangers and servants in a strange land, since Joseph seems to promise nothing but pleasures. Moses says nothing, but Calvin conjectures that Jacob was not forgetful of it; for unless he had been retained by some celestial chain he could never have remained in Egypt after the scarcity was over, since by remaining voluntarily he would have appeared to cast away the hope of the inheritance. Seeing that he does not provide for his return but only commands his corpse to be carried thither, nor exhorts his sons to return but suffers them to settle, he does this not from indolence, but because he is preparing himself and his offspring to bear that tyranny of which Isaac had forewarned him. Gill identifies Goshen with the Heliopolitan nome, which Strabo reckoned to be in Arabia, and wonders whether Joseph had a grant of it or whether it was the domain of his father-in-law the priest of On.

Clarke supposes the district had been allotted to Joseph by the king, since otherwise he could scarcely have promised it without Pharaoh's consent; it was the most easterly province of Lower Egypt, lying next to Canaan, and is also called the land of Rameses from a city of that name. Because the Hebrew for rain is a similar word, Jerome and others supposed Goshen was so named because it had rain, unlike Egypt in general, and being watered from heaven might account for its being the best of the land. Clarke thinks Joseph laid considerable stress on speaking with his brethren in Hebrew without an interpreter, as the Targum of Jonathan renders it, that it was his own mouth that spoke with them in the language of the house of the sanctuary; and he notes that among the Asiatics kissing the beard, neck and shoulders is in use to this day, so that falling on the neck signifies no more than kissing it with the arms around. Wesley says that if the brothers could recollect themselves they might remember something of his features and speech.

Ellicott places Goshen on the eastern bank of the Nile, commencing a little north of Memphis and extending to the Mediterranean; it was probably an unsettled district, rich in pastures, belonging in a very loose way to Egypt, and there the Israelites were constantly joined by Semitic immigrants enrolled among their dependants. He reckons the household that would come down with Jacob: as the famine had lasted only two years and he had preserved his flocks, he had probably lost few of his servants, and would go down as head of a large tribe called Israelites after him — a name of subjection as much as of descent. Keil marks the sequence at the end: only after Joseph had by a triple assurance dispelled their fear of retribution, and sealed his words by embracing and kissing them with tears, did his brethren talk with him.

outliers.note: reads the household as a tribe of dependants, so that Israelite is from the first a name of subjection as much as of descent

16.pericope_label: Pharaoh's invitation: regard not your stuff

schools.summary: Calvin points out that the order of the narrative is not the order of events: before Joseph sent for his father the report of his brethren's coming had reached the palace, and he would not have promised them a home so confidently except by the king's permission; the king had with a ready mind declared his esteem for Joseph by freely offering his father and brethren the most fertile part of Egypt. From another statement of Moses it appears that as long as this king lived the Israelites were treated with clemency, the beginning of the tyranny being ascribed to his successor, to whom Joseph was unknown. Gill supposes the report reached court from some of Joseph's household who had overheard what passed, and that Joseph afterwards waited on Pharaoh himself, the king being unlikely to give such orders on a rumour; and he records a contrary construction of the command about their goods, that the words mean rather to leave nothing behind but bring all away, as though Joseph would not have them think of returning, though he judges it agrees less well with what follows.

Henry dwells on Pharaoh's kindness to Joseph and, for his sake, to his relations. He bade the brethren welcome though it was a time of scarcity and they were likely to be a charge to him; and because it pleased Pharaoh it pleased his servants too, or at least they pretended so. He promised every convenience for the removal and the settlement: if the good of all the land of Egypt would suffice them they were welcome to it all, even the fat of the land. Pharaoh was respectful to Joseph in gratitude, since the neighbours would say that surely the Egyptians are a wise people to be so well stocked in a time of scarcity; and there is a gratitude owing even to inferiors, to be requited not only to our benefactors but to their relations. What they had in Canaan Henry reckoned but stuff beside what awaited them: those for whom Christ intends shares in his heavenly glory ought not to regard the stuff of this world, for its best enjoyments are but stuff, but lumber, which we cannot make sure of here, much less carry away; better things are reserved in that blessed land whither our Joseph has gone to prepare a place.

Clarke renders the command about their goods literally, let not your eye spare your vessels, a general term taking in household furniture and agricultural utensils: they were not to encumber themselves with articles readily found in Egypt.

Ellicott sees the point of recording the welcome so fully: it mattered greatly for their future position that the Israelites should go into Egypt not as men who had forced themselves on the country but as invited guests. On the wagons he speaks from the monuments — Egypt being flat and carefully cultivated was adapted for vehicles, those depicted having two wheels and being drawn by oxen, while the chariots of Pharaoh and Joseph were probably drawn by horses, then newly introduced — and he distinguishes the little ones from the household, the Hebrew covering the whole mass of dependants, so that where the household means chiefly the men, this term would be the female slaves and the children. Keil notes that Egypt was from time immemorial rich in small two-wheeled carriages usable even where there were no roads, and that Pharaoh empowered Joseph to give his brethren such carriages for the children, the wives and their aged father.

outliers.note: marks the political importance of the invitation: Israel enters Egypt as invited guests, not as men who forced themselves on the country

21.pericope_label: See that ye fall not out by the way

schools.summary: Calvin asks why Joseph loaded his brethren with money and garments when they would soon return, and answers that he did it on account of his father and their wives, that they might be the less reluctant to leave Canaan; for he knew his message would scarcely be believed unless manifest tokens of its truth were presented. On the changes of raiment he differs from the tradition: Jerome translated the phrase two robes, and others follow him, but Calvin supposes rather elegant garments such as were used at weddings and on festal days. On the parting caution he notes that the Hebrew word may mean either to tremble or to make a tumult, and thinks the latter the more appropriate: Joseph was pacified towards them, but admonishes them not to stir up strife, since each, in excusing himself, would be likely to lay the blame on others — and Christ requires his disciples to be not only lovers of peace but peace-makers. Of Jacob's fainting he says it was no simple affection of joy but a mingled perturbation: Moses does not say he was suffocated by sudden gladness, as some suppose, but that having no confidence in his sons he was held in suspense between hope and fear. Gill supposes what the brothers reported was not their selling of him, which Jacob perhaps never heard, but Joseph's advancement.

Henry, with Wesley after him, knows the brethren were too apt to be quarrelsome, and that what had lately passed might give them occasion; so Joseph, having forgiven them all, lays them under an obligation not to upbraid each other. This charge our Lord has given us too, that whatever former occurrences are remembered we fall not out — for we are brethren and have all one Father; we are guilty, verily guilty, and have more reason to fall out with ourselves; and we are by the way, a way that lies through Egypt, where many eyes seek advantage against us, and leads to Canaan, where we hope to be for ever in perfect peace. On the homecoming Henry marks two stages. The relation of it at first sank Jacob's spirits: when without any preamble his sons came in crying that Joseph was yet alive, perhaps he thought they bantered him, or the mention of the name revived his sorrow, so that his heart fainted — that Joseph is alive is too good news to be true, and he faints because he believes it not, for we faint because we do not believe. But with the wagons before him Jacob is called Israel again, for he begins to recover his wonted vigour: it pleases him to think that Joseph is alive, and he says nothing of the glory they had told him of, for it was enough to him that Joseph was alive — and those who would be content with less degrees of comfort are best prepared for greater.

Clarke sets the gifts among Eastern usages, since the Asiatic sovereigns keep hundreds of changes of raiment ready as presents for those they honour. On Jacob's recovery he notes that the Greek word for his reviving signifies the blowing up of almost extinguished embers, the word Paul uses for stirring up the gift of God.

Ellicott says the brethren would show by their very apparel how honourable their treatment had been, and reports that several moderns render the parting caution be not afraid of the journey, but on insufficient grounds. He reads Jacob's fainting as surprise rather than incredulity: crushed by the loss of the child who had taken Rachel's place, he could not open his mind to the tidings, whose first effect was to chill him with a renewed sense of loss. Keil says his heart did not beat at the news, for he put no faith in it.

28.pericope_label: It is enough; I will go and see him before I die

schools.summary: Gill takes the exclamation as the Targums do, that the word is much or great and that Jacob had much joy — it was more to him than all Joseph's splendour that he was in the land of the living. Though his age was great and the journey long, so strong was his desire of seeing Joseph that he determined at once upon going, expecting death shortly; and Gill supposes the resolution made in submission to God's will, since he wished to live only to enjoy this favour. He ends by making Joseph in this disclosure a type of Christ, who manifests himself to his people and not to the world.

Clarke insists that what moved the old man was not the dignity but the life, and closes the chapter with four reflections on Joseph's conduct. It is strange that he never took one of the many opportunities to let his father know he was alive, since his father would undoubtedly have paid his ransom; but prudence dictated secrecy, for his brethren, jealous in the extreme, would soon have found other methods of destroying his life had they got him again into their power, so that for his safety he chose rather to be a bond-slave in Egypt. His carriage to his brethren before making himself known appears inexcusably harsh, if not vindictive, but when the men are considered no other means would have awakened their torpid consciences — a desperate disease requires a desperate remedy. The hardest of the four is the demand that Benjamin be torn away from an aged and desolate father: unless the Spirit of prophecy had assured him the experiment would end favourably his conduct cannot well be vindicated, and this consideration, if it does not untie the knot, at least cuts it. Perhaps it is best to say that Joseph acted as directed by a providence under whose influence he might have been led to do many things he had not designed. Of the chapter itself Clarke speaks warmly: Joseph's speech is inferior only to Judah's in the chapter before, the whole heart of the affectionate brother being seen in the delicacy of his apology for them, and the chapter is a masterpiece, the more impressive because it is evidently a simple relation of facts just as they occurred.

Ellicott would not lay too much stress on the change of name, as though Israel were a title fit only for the patriarch's happier hours, since it is given him earlier in the chapter in the midst of his distress, both names being long in use of him personally. But because Israel alone was the name given to Jacob's family, a high significance was plainly attached to it, and the inheritance of the Abrahamic promises was early connected with it.

outliers.note: defends Joseph's long silence and his harshness as prudence and remedy, and reads the demand for Benjamin as intelligible only under a prophetic intimation
